terms.grammar: noun phrase: praefectus, praefectī m., with the dative urbī
terms.comment: Traupman’s word for a modern mayor, and Morgan–Owens’s first (as urbis praefectus, after Vives). Classically the prefect of the city of Rome: under the Republic the consuls’ deputy while they were away, under the emperors a standing office with its own jurisdiction (Lewis & Short, s.v. praeficiō). A Roman town had no single mayor, but two magistrates elected for a year, the duovirī.

terms.gloss: the two chief magistrates of a Roman town
terms.comment: The highest magistrates of the mūnicipia and colonies (Lewis & Short, who head the word duovir and call duumvir less correct). The nearest Roman thing to a mayor; at Capua they wanted to be called praetors instead (Cic. Agr. 2.93).

terms.gloss: the head of a ward or a village
terms.grammar: noun phrase: magister, magistrī m., with the genitive vīcī
evidence: Suet. Aug. 30: hōs magistrī ē plēbe cujusque vīcīniae lēctī
terms.comment: At Rome the overseers of the city’s wards (vīcī), chosen from the people of each neighbourhood (Suet. Aug. 30; Lewis & Short, s.v. magister). A vīcus is also a village, so the title suits a village mayor; Morgan–Owens lists it among the words for a mayor.
The title from which English mayor and French maire come; Traupman lists it. In classical Latin it is only the comparative, greater or elder.

terms.gloss: mayor; a woman mayor, magistra urbis
terms.comment: Andresian’s phrase, with magistra urbis for a woman; not a Roman title. The Roman model is magister vīcī above.

phrases.latin: Immō proavus tuus ōlim erat praefectus urbī.
phrases.english: Well, your great-grandfather was once mayor of the city.
